message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, the line shouldn't run as written. It's medically wrong, and it gives staff advice that won't help them.

**Why it's wrong**

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.** They don't treat flu, shorten it or ease the symptoms. Doctors generally won't prescribe them for flu itself.
- **Antibiotics carry real downsides.** Side effects such as stomach upset and allergic reactions are common. Unnecessary use also adds to antibiotic resistance, which is why health services actively discourage requesting them for colds and flu.
- **Antiviral medicines for flu do exist,** such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu). They're mainly for people at higher risk of complications, work best when started within about 48 hours, and on average shorten illness by around a day. They aren't a general "back to work sooner" fix.

**Why his GP may have prescribed them**

Flu can sometimes lead to a *secondary bacterial infection*, such as a chest infection, pneumonia or sinusitis, and antibiotics are appropriate for those. His GP may have been treating one of these, or a different illness. Either way, his experience doesn't support a general tip, and you can say this to him without implying he's misremembering.

**Suggested replacement**

> If you come down with flu, rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids and use paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches and fever. Stay home until you're feeling better, so you don't pass it on to colleagues. Antibiotics won't help with flu itself, because it's caused by a virus. Contact your GP or NHS 111 if you're struggling to breathe, have chest pain, feel worse after starting to recover, or are in a higher-risk group, such as being pregnant or having a long-term condition.
>
> The best protection is the flu jab. [If applicable: the company offers free vaccinations. Details at…]

The flu-jab point makes a better headline tip than the original. It's well supported and it actually reduces time off work.
